title: Race relations and white musicians in Birmingham
summary: He says he stayed on campus and did not think about race then, never played with white musicians, and notes Birmingham's good black and white players.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, at this time too. What, did you have any idea of black-white relations in Birmingham? Was there anything there that....?

You know, I really didn't. I didn't get into that. You know, cause like I say, I didn't have to go through, I played for white affairs. But, you know, I was young and everything. So, we played. We did what we were supposed to do. And the ones I knew, we talked and everything. And when we finished, well, we'd go on back to the school. But, I didn't know, I didn't know too much. I didn't have too much. You know, I didn't get into that too much. Like, because like I said, I stayed there. And when I got to 'Bama State, I was on the campus there. But, I
did have to go downtown and everything. But, I never got in no trouble. I didn't think about it too much at that time.
I actually started thinking about it as the years went along.
Did you have very much of an idea of what was going on in the white communities at this time? Musically?

No, I didn't. I didn't know too much, you know. But, it's like I said. I didn't get a chance to play with none of the white musicians at that time. I played when I first, I met some at 'Bama State. That's in Montgomery. when we started, when I was there I started meeting a few of the fellows.

And, we used to talk music. You know, but we didn't get a chance to play together at that time. Then, I met, I met, after 'Bama State, I went back to Birmingham and I began to meet a few there. You know, then, it was like I said. We didn't get a chance to play
with each other, but we talked music and we knew of each other. Like that, the local radio station used to broadcast, some used to broadcast on the local stations.
Were you aware at that time of any different approaches or ways of playing the music or styles or anything like that?

No. At that time, it seemed like what they had on paper, that's how they played. Played it nice and straight. Not, nothing like jazz, you know. Whatever notes they had down there, they played them that way. But, Birmingham had a lot of good musicians, black and white. And, you know, a lot of black musicians and white musicians came from Birmingham to New York to get into big times. Now, I didn't know about that before I got there.
Well, one last thing before we sort of move onto, oh...
